course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 1
unit.description: Follow Native American societies, European exploration, the Columbian Exchange, and the Spanish empire from 1491 to 1607.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans
lesson.summary: How Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans misunderstood and borrowed from one another, how Native peoples defended their lands, and how Spanish leaders argued over the treatment of Native peoples.
learningGoals: Explain how differing views of land, gender, family, religion, and power led to misunderstandings between Europeans and Native Americans.
Explain how Native peoples used diplomacy and military resistance to defend their sovereignty.
Explain how Spanish leaders debated the treatment of Native peoples and how justifications for subjugation evolved.
lesson.bigIdea: Europeans and Native Americans held divergent worldviews, borrowed useful things from each other, and clashed over land and labor, while Europeans argued over how non-Europeans should be treated.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain how and why perspectives of others developed and changed. Look for what each side believed, what each side wanted, and how each side acted on those beliefs.

sections.title: Misunderstandings and borrowing

blocks.text: In the early years of contact, each group tried to make sense of the other using its own assumptions. Europeans and Native Americans held divergent views about land use, gender roles, family, religion, and power, and these differences often produced misunderstandings.

Many Europeans believed land could be owned by individuals, fenced, bought, and sold. Many Native societies instead recognized shared rights to use land for farming, hunting, and gathering, and they did not see an agreement as giving up the land forever. Europeans also noticed that in many Native societies women farmed while men hunted and fought. Because European custom treated farming as men's work, many colonists judged Native societies as disordered or uncivilized. Native peoples often saw trade as a way to build lasting relationships through gifts and alliances, while Europeans emphasized profit.

Over time each side also adopted useful parts of the other's culture. Europeans learned to grow maize and other Native crops, and they borrowed Native knowledge of the land and its waters. Native peoples acquired European metal tools, cloth, and firearms, and, on the Plains, horses.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Misunderstanding did not mean that only Europeans failed to understand. Both sides misread the other, and each also borrowed what it found useful.

sections.takeaway: Different views of land, gender, religion, and trade produced misunderstandings, but each side also borrowed from the other.

sections.title: Diplomacy and resistance

blocks.text: As Europeans pressed onto Native lands and demanded Native labor, Native peoples worked to defend their political independence, their economies, their religious beliefs, and their ideas about gender relations. They used two main approaches: diplomatic negotiation and military resistance.

Diplomacy included trade agreements and alliances. Some Native leaders allied with Europeans to gain advantages over their own rivals. The Tlaxcalans, for example, joined Cortés against the Aztecs, whose tribute demands they resented. Military resistance took many forms. In 1598 Spanish settlers under Juan de Oñate entered the Pueblo lands of New Mexico and demanded food, goods, and labor. When warriors from Acoma Pueblo killed a group of Oñate's men, the Spanish attacked in January 1599, destroyed the pueblo, and enslaved many survivors.

blocks.title: Cause and effect
blocks.text: European demands for land, labor, and religious change led Native peoples to negotiate when they could and to fight when they felt they must.

sections.takeaway: Native peoples defended their sovereignty through alliances and negotiation and through armed resistance.

sections.title: The Spanish debate over treatment

blocks.text: Extended contact with Native Americans and Africans led Spanish religious and political leaders to argue over how non-Europeans should be treated. The Spanish Crown claimed the right to rule the Americas and to spread Christianity, and in 1513 royal lawyers drafted a document called the Requerimiento, which conquerors were told to read aloud to Native peoples. It demanded that they accept Spanish rule and the Christian faith or face war.

Some Spaniards condemned the cruelty of the colonial system. The Dominican friar Bartolomé de las Casas, who had seen the abuse of Native workers, argued that Native peoples were rational human beings who should be converted by persuasion, not by force. His writings influenced the New Laws of 1542, which restricted new encomiendas and tried to limit abuse, though colonists resisted and enforcement was weak. Las Casas at first suggested that enslaved Africans could ease the burden on Native workers, a view he later condemned. Others, such as the scholar Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, argued that Native peoples were naturally inferior and could justly be ruled and made to work. The two men presented their arguments in a famous debate at Valladolid in 1550–1551.

Over time, the justifications used to subjugate Native Americans and Africans changed and combined religious, cultural, and racial arguments. Defenders of conquest and slavery claimed they were civilizing and converting people they described as inferior, and these ideas about race became more important as slavery expanded.

sections.takeaway: Spanish leaders disagreed about how to treat Native peoples, and the justifications for subjugating Africans and Native Americans came to include religious, cultural, and racial arguments.

connections.title: From cultural contact to causation
connections.body: Topics 1.1 through 1.6 describe contact, conquest, and the social order that followed. Topic 1.7 asks you to explain how and why those developments happened and what they caused.
connections.transferQuestion: How did European views of land and gender contribute to conflict with Native peoples?
connections.feedback: A strong answer names a specific difference, such as individual ownership versus shared use, and explains how it produced misunderstanding or conflict over land and labor.
